title: The Seeing-Nature Is the Mind
author: Mingde
excerpt: [Ānanda, you answered me earlier that you see my radiant fist. Where does this fist’s radiance come from? How does it become a fist? With what do you see it? Ānanda said: Because the Buddha’s whole body is like Jambu-river gold, glowing (xì) like a jeweled mountain, born of purity, it has radiance. I actually saw with my eyes the five wheel-fingered tips bend and clench to show people, and so there is the appearance of a fist.]

inline.s: (The original text is excerpted from the Śūraṅgama Sutra)

[Ānanda, you answered me earlier that you see my radiant fist. Where does this fist’s radiance come from? How does it become a fist? With what do you see it? Ānanda said: Because the Buddha’s whole body is like Jambu-river gold, glowing
like a jeweled mountain, born of purity, it has radiance. I actually saw with my eyes the five wheel-fingered tips bend and clench to show people, and so there is the appearance of a fist.]

Ānanda, you answered me earlier that you saw my radiant fist. Now then, why does this fist have radiance? How does it come to be a fist? With what do you see it?’ Ānanda said: ‘Because the Buddha’s whole body is like Jambu-river gold, radiant like a jeweled mountain, pure and undefiled, the fist has radiance. I saw with my eyes the Buddha bend his five fingers into a fist to show people, and so there is the appearance of a fist.’

[Jambu-river gold] “Jambu” (yánfú) is the name of a tree; “dan” (tán) is a transliteration whose meaning is “river.” Beneath the Jambu tree there is a river called “Jambudan,” and the gold produced in this river is called Jambu-river gold. This gold is reddish-yellow in color, with a purple flame-like sheen. [Wheel-fingers] The Buddha’s fingertips all bear the marks of a thousand-spoked wheel, and so his fingers are called wheel-fingers. [Bend and clench] to bend the fingers and clench them into a fist.

[The Buddha told Ānanda: Today the Tathāgata tells you in truth that even the wise must rely on similes to attain awakening. Ānanda, take my fist: if I had no hand, there would be no fist; and if you had no eye, there would be no seeing of yours. If you compare your eye-faculty with the principle of my fist, are they alike in meaning? Ānanda said: Yes, World-Honored One! Since without my eye there would be no seeing of mine, to compare my eye-faculty with the Tathāgata’s fist — the matter and its principle are alike.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘Now I tell you in truth that even the wise must rely on similes to attain awakening, to say nothing of those without wisdom. (Therefore, below, the World-Honored One uses similes to clarify the Buddha’s principle.) Ānanda, take my fist: if I had no hand, there would be no fist; and if you had no eye, there would be no seeing of yours. Compare your seeing with my making of the fist — are they the same in principle?’ Ānanda said: ‘Yes, World-Honored One! If I had no eye, there would be no seeing of mine; if you had no hand, there would be no fist of yours. The principle of the two is the same.’

[The Buddha told Ānanda: You say they are alike, but this is not so. Why? A man without a hand has no fist at all, but a man without eyes is not wholly without seeing. Why is this? Try asking a blind man on the road: What do you see? Those blind men will surely answer you: Before my eyes now I see only darkness, and nothing else. Judging from this, since the objects before them are themselves dark, how is their seeing deficient? Ānanda said: The blind see only darkness before their eyes — how can that be called seeing? The Buddha told Ānanda: When the blind, who have no eyes, see only darkness, and a sighted person in a dark room also sees only darkness — are the two darknesses different, or not different? Ānanda said: World-Honored One, comparing the darkness of the man in the dark with that of the blind, there is no difference at all.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘You say the principle of the two is the same, but that is not right. Why? A man without a hand can never have a fist, but a man without eyes is not wholly without seeing. Why do I say this? If on the road you ask a blind man, “What do you see?”, those blind men will surely answer: “Now before my eyes I see only a stretch of darkness, and nothing else.” From this we know that it is the objects before them that are dark — so what is deficient in their seeing?’ Ānanda said: ‘Before the blind there is only a stretch of darkness — how can it be called seeing?’ The Buddha told Ānanda: ‘The blind, who have no eyes, see only darkness; and a sighted person in a dark room sees only darkness. Are these two darknesses different, or not different?’ Ānanda said: ‘World-Honored One, these two darknesses are exactly the same.’

[Ānanda! If a man without eyes, seeing only darkness before him, suddenly gains eyesight, and then, regarding the objects before him, sees various forms, this is called seeing by the eye. But the man in the dark, seeing only darkness before him, suddenly gains lamplight, and then, regarding the objects before him, sees various forms — should this not be called seeing by the lamp? If the lamp sees, then the lamp is able to see, and so it would not be called a lamp. Moreover, if the lamp sees, what has it to do with you? Therefore you should know: the lamp can reveal forms, and the one who sees is the eye, not the lamp; the eye can reveal forms,
but the seeing-nature is the mind, not the eye

Ānanda! If a man without eyes, seeing only darkness before him, suddenly gains eyes, and then, regarding the objects before him, sees various things (forms), and this is called seeing by the eye; then the man in the dark room, seeing only darkness before him, suddenly gains lamplight, and then, regarding the objects before him, sees various things — this should be called seeing by the lamp. If it is seeing by the lamp, meaning the lamp can see, then it would not be called a lamp (for a thing that illuminates things is called a lamp, while a thing that can see things is called an eye). Moreover, if the lamp sees, what has that to do with your eye? From this we know: the lamp can reveal things (reveal forms), and what thus sees is the eye, not the lamp; the eye can reveal things, but what truly sees (the seeing-nature) is the mind, not the organ of the eye.’
[See various forms] see various things. Here “form” (sè) refers to all matter that has shape and occupies space.
